analysis.one_liner: Gives bank customers the right to stop banks from sharing their financial records, including with corporate affiliates.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 29 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent, but the House Banking and Commerce Committees never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: A year after Congress passed the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, banks could share customers' personal financial information with their own corporate affiliates without asking. This bill would have changed that: customers could say no to sharing with affiliates as well as outside companies, banks would need explicit consent before selling detailed records of a person's spending, health information could not be used to decide who gets credit, and customers would gain the right to see and correct the files banks keep on them. It also let state attorneys general sue to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a bank account, credit card, or brokerage account. The bill would have given customers a say over whether their bank shares their records with corporate affiliates, blocked banks from transferring lists of individual customers' transactions for marketing, barred banks from using health information to decide whether to offer someone credit or on what terms, and let customers see and correct their own information.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing right to opt out of information sharing to corporate affiliates, not just outside companies, and requires the opt-out to be as convenient as the notice itself [S3].

Prohibits banks from transferring individualized lists of a customer's transactions or interests, and lists containing identifiable health information, unless the customer affirmatively consents [S3].

Bars financial institutions from obtaining or using individually identifiable health information when deciding whether to offer, price, or continue a financial product, except with consent and only if the same information is required of all customers [S3].

Gives consumers the right to access information a financial institution holds about them and to dispute and correct material that is inaccurate or incomplete, with an exemption for proprietary credit-scoring algorithms [S3].

Bans disclosure of customers' account or access numbers to affiliates or third parties, tightens limits on redisclosure by companies that receive the data, and moves privacy notices to before a customer relationship begins [S3].
Adds enforcement teeth: makes violations an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act and empowers state attorneys general to sue on behalf of residents for violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, insurers, and other financial institutions, which would face compliance costs and lose the ability to freely pool and market customer data across corporate affiliates; also data brokers and marketers who buy customer transaction lists from banks.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on financial institutions of every size, including community banks and credit unions, which would have to build notice, consent-tracking, and access/correction systems across overlapping federal regulators [S3].

The core protection is an opt-out, not an opt-in: banks could still share most data with affiliates unless the customer affirmatively said no, and many customers never see or act on opt-out notices; only spending-habit data and health information require affirmative consent [S3].

The bill preserves broad exceptions, letting institutions share information to service accounts, market their own products to their own customers, run shared call centers, and work with attorneys, accountants, and auditors [S3].
Consumers could be charged a reasonable fee to access their own information, though the charge must be disclosed first [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and would have shifted power over financial data from institutions to the people the data describes. The weaknesses are that the main sharing right still starts from 'yes by default' rather than 'no by default', the list of exceptions is long, and compliance costs would hit small institutions too. On balance, the benefits to customers' control over their own financial and health records outweigh the compliance burden, though a stronger bill would have required consent before any sharing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Banking and Commerce Committees and their subcommittees on the day it was introduced, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce, the top Democrat on the House Banking Committee, introduced the bill on May 4, 2000 with 21 original cosponsors [S1].

The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services and the Committee on Commerce, and to the subcommittees on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and on Finance and Hazardous Materials [S5].
The bill reached 29 cosponsors, 28 Democrats and one Independent, but no action appears in the record after the referrals [S4].
The 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 without the bill receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions kept the ability to share customer records with corporate affiliates without asking, and marketers kept access to customer transaction data. Consumers kept only the weaker privacy rules of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which required notices and opt-outs for sharing with outside companies but not affiliates.

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.role: Ranking Democrat, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the Banking Committee's Democratic members as cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jim Leach
against.role: Chairman, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed strengthening the affiliate-sharing rules of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which they had sought so they could combine customer data across insurance, securities, and banking affiliates.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored, and the Republican committee chairmen took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to share customer records with corporate affiliates without a customer's say-so, restricted sale of transaction lists, and barred use of health information in credit decisions. The affiliate-sharing right they defended came from the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, whose value depends on using customer data customers cannot easily see or contest.
They buy individualized lists of bank customers' transactions and preferences; the bill would have required each customer's affirmative consent before such lists were transferred.
Their customers gain privacy protections, but the institutions would bear the same compliance burden as large banks for building notice, consent, and access-and-correction systems.
